## 6. Anticipated Authoritative Guidance and Pending Regulatory Events

One pending event is written into the Decision. The authorisation can stop early: «However, in the event that the Council, acting on the basis of Article 113 TFEU or any other relevant provision of the TFEU, introduces new minimum levels of taxation as referred to in Article 7 of Directive 2003/96/EC for gas oil and unleaded petrol used as motor fuels to which the authorisation granted in Article 1 of this Decision would not be adapted, this Decision shall cease to apply on the date on which those new minimum levels of taxation become applicable.» The text gives no date for any such Council act, so 30 November 2026 is the latest end the Decision states.

*Analytical inference:* the end of the authorisation depends on a Council decision on new minimum levels that the text does not date, so a cost built on the lower duty carries that early-stop risk until 30 November 2026. The text does not state what Swedish rate would apply after either stop.

## 7. Threshold Questions

Two points decide whether a fuel falls under the Decision. The fuels are named: «for gas oil and unleaded petrol used as motor fuels». The size of the cut is capped by the Article 1 text above.

*Analytical inference:* the Decision does not define gas oil, unleaded petrol or motor fuels, and states no Swedish rate, so which Swedish fuel purchases carry the lower duty is not stated. *Legal Confirmation Required:* whether a fuel bought for a refrigeration unit or other non-propulsion use on a vehicle counts as used as motor fuel.

## 8. Substantive Requirements

Authorisation. «Sweden is authorised to apply a reduction of the rates up to 2,4 SEK per litre below the minimum levels of taxation referred to in Article 7 of Directive 2003/96/EC for gas oil and unleaded petrol used as motor fuels.»

Period. «This Decision shall apply from 1 July 2026 until 30 November 2026.»

Taking effect. «This Decision shall take effect on the date of its notification.»

Addressee. «This Decision is addressed to the Kingdom of Sweden.»

The Decision states no penalty, fine or sanction and names no enforcement body.

*Analytical inference:* the Decision creates a permission for Sweden and a time limit, and states no duty on a fuel buyer, carrier or forwarder. The date of notification, from which the Decision takes effect, is not stated in the text.

*Legal Confirmation Required:* whether the Decision, addressed to Sweden, creates any duty or charge for a forwarder or its client.

No phase-in is stated in Articles 1 to 4. No exceptions are stated in Articles 1 to 4. No scope limits are stated in Articles 1 to 4 other than the State and the fuels named in Article 1.

Obligations surveyed: 4; workspace-adjacent: 0; extracted as FACT: 4.
Shortfall: the Decision has four Articles, all four are extracted, and the text states no further obligation.

The only filing the Decision records is Sweden's own request: «By letter dated 26 March 2026, in accordance with Article 19 of Directive 2003/96/EC, the Swedish authorities requested authorisation to apply reduced rates of excise duty to gas oil and unleaded petrol used as motor fuels.»

*Analytical inference:* the four Articles name no registration or reporting step for a fuel buyer, carrier or forwarder. *Legal Confirmation Required:* whether Swedish national rules attach any record-keeping to the lower duty for a business that buys fuel in Sweden.

## 11. Operational System Requirements

WINDOW CLOSING: the Decision asks for no system, but it sets a fixed period: «This Decision shall apply from 1 July 2026 until 30 November 2026.» A rate table or quote tool that carries a Swedish fuel cost has to show that period or it will keep the lower duty after the authorisation ends.

- A pricing-data owner adds a valid-until date of 30 November 2026 to each Swedish fuel cost entry that assumes the lower duty, so the entry is reviewed on that date.

*Analytical inference:* this rests on Article 2; the text states no data duty on a forwarder.

## 12. Exemptions and Edge Cases

The Council keeps other EU rules in force: «This Decision is without prejudice to the application of Union rules regarding State aid».

*Analytical inference:* a State aid assessment is a separate matter from this authorisation, and the text does not say how it would affect Sweden's reduced rates. *Legal Confirmation Required:* whether any State aid question attaches to the Swedish reduction for a business that benefits from it.

   "body": "## 1. Purpose and Scope of This Document

This brief covers the Chinese guideline that sets the course of the national carbon trading market: «The guideline is jointly issued by the General Office of the Communist Party of China Central Committee and the General Office of the State Council.» Its reach is national: «China has unveiled a guideline to accelerate the country's green and low-carbon transition and strengthen the construction of the national carbon trading market». It is a policy guideline called the Opinions in the captures, so it sets direction and dates, and detailed rules are still to be written. What the captures state is quoted between guillemets; what it means for a freight operator is marked *Analytical inference:* and each point for counsel is marked *Legal Confirmation Required:*.

*Analytical inference:* the guideline is addressed to Chinese authorities and emitters. It names no freight forwarder, carrier or shipper, so a freight business meets it through carriers, producers and cargo owners that fall under the scheme.

## 2. What This Regulation Is and Why It Applies to the Workspace

The guideline widens China's national emissions trading scheme. The aim in the government's own report: «It states that by 2027, the country's carbon trading market will encompass all major industrial sectors, and the national voluntary greenhouse gas emission reduction trading market will expand to include all key fields.» A policy group describes it the same way: «By 2027, the National ETS is expected to cover all major industrial emitters.» The Opinions are dated: «On 25 August 2025», and the capture states no date on which this guideline enters into force: «Updated: August 25, 2025 21:54 Xinhua BEIJING, Aug. 25» The record's stored date of 1 January 2025 is therefore not relied on here.

Which sectors are next is not fixed: «While the Opinions do not specify which sectors will be prioritized, civil aviation, copper smelting, flat glass, petrochemicals, chemicals, and paper manufacturing have already undergone a decade of greenhouse gas data monitoring, reporting, and verification (MRV).» A law and business adviser adds the consequence for companies: «foreign firms in sectors that could be affected, in particular petrochemicals, nonferrous metals, and aviation, will come under the purview of the ETS.»

*Analytical inference:* aviation is the sector closest to freight that the captures name as a likely entrant, so air carriers serving China may face allowance and reporting duties when it joins; steel, aluminium and cement producers are already inside the scheme. The captures name no freight forwarder duty.

## 3. Issues Requiring Immediate Action

MONITORING: no step falls on a freight business within the next 30 days, and the detailed rules are still to come. An air-freight desk asks, at its next rate review with each carrier that flies from Chinese airports, whether the carrier expects its flights to be covered when civil aviation joins the scheme and whether an allowance cost would be added to rates. An export desk lists China-origin steel, aluminium and cement shipments bound for Europe and asks each shipper whether ETS coverage changes its exposure to the EU border carbon charge, because «Industries covered by the ETS might be able to avoid CBAM charges when exporting to Europe».

The coverage date is the one to plan around: «By 2027, the National ETS is expected to cover all major industrial emitters.»

*Analytical inference:* both questions rest on the sector names and the CBAM sentence above; the captures state no pass-through of any allowance cost to freight rates, so the answers have to come from carriers and shippers.

## 4. How the Workspace Sits in the Compliance Chain

The captures describe who carries the duties today: «The ETS covers key emissions units, companies whose annual greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions exceed 26,000 tons of CO2 equivalent (CO2e).» They are «responsible for controlling their emissions, reporting verified carbon data, surrendering allowances, disclosing trading activity, and complying with oversight from provincial and national ecological and environmental authorities.» The authority is named: «Ministry of Ecology and Environment (MEE)». A forwarder, carrier or shipper is not named.

*Analytical inference:* a freight business is outside the compliance chain; its carriers and the producers whose cargo it moves may be inside it. *Legal Confirmation Required:* whether a particular Chinese carrier or producer on a client's route is a covered emitter, which only the covered-entity lists of the authority can show.

## 6. Anticipated Authoritative Guidance and Pending Regulatory Events

The detailed rules are still to be written: «In accordance with the requirements set out in the Opinions, the MEE, in collaboration with other relevant ministries and agencies, will develop and implement detailed supporting policies and measures to carry out the guidelines.» The cap is a later step: «Starting as early as 2027, sectors with relatively stable emissions profiles will be subject to absolute cap controls.»

*Analytical inference:* the supporting policies are the point where sectors, thresholds and allowance rules become fixed; until they appear the captures give no sector list and no rate effect.

## 7. Threshold Questions

Two questions decide who is in scope. The first is which sectors join: «The Opinions call for the orderly inclusion of additional sectors and greenhouse gases in the National ETS, guided by factors such as sectoral emissions, data quality, and abatement potential.» The second is the size line for an emitter, which the captures give for the scheme as it stands: «companies whose annual greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions exceed 26,000 tons of CO2 equivalent (CO2e)».

*Analytical inference:* the captures do not say whether the size line stays the same for new sectors. *Legal Confirmation Required:* whether an operator or its client meets the emitter definition for a new sector once the supporting rules are published.

## 8. Substantive Requirements

Coverage. «By 2027, the National ETS is expected to cover all major industrial emitters.» The record stores the 2027 coverage target as 1 January 2027, the first day of the year; the captures give the year only.

Caps. «Starting as early as 2027, sectors with relatively stable emissions profiles will be subject to absolute cap controls.» The effect: «At that point, increases in production by covered entities will no longer automatically result in higher allowance allocations.»

Allocation. «the allocation mechanism will evolve from primarily free allocation to a hybrid model incorporating auctioning of allowances, with the aim of improving market efficiency and price discovery.» For the three industries added in 2024, cement, steel and aluminum smelting, a phased step is set: «with a phased transition to intensity-based allocation tied to production output planned for 2025 to 2026».

Cap-and-trade. «By 2030, China aims to have a cap-and-trade system with a mix of allocation and auctioning, and a voluntary market that is credible, transparent, widely participatory, and aligned with international standards.»

Voluntary credits. «expanding the CCER to cover emission-reduction projects across “all key fields” by 2027, and establishing a national voluntary greenhouse gas emission reduction trading market by 2030».

Reporting and disclosure. «Strengthened transparency: Emitters, registries, exchanges, and financial institutions must disclose emissions, trading, and compliance data.»

Scope. «Expansion of scope The Opinions call for the orderly inclusion of additional sectors and greenhouse gases in the National ETS».

Penalty. The captures state no penalty, fine or sanction for an emitter that does not meet these duties.

*Analytical inference:* every duty above falls on a covered emitter, the market operators or the authority; none falls on a freight business. No exceptions are stated in the captured text of the Opinions.

*Legal Confirmation Required:* whether the supporting policies place a duty on a carrier or forwarder that handles cargo for a covered producer.

## 10. Registration and Reporting Obligations

Covered emitters already report: «reporting verified carbon data, surrendering allowances, disclosing trading activity». The Opinions add: «Advanced MRV systems: Digital registries and automated monitoring will be rolled out, with stricter accreditation for verification bodies.» The expected effect for companies: «Companies can expect an increased compliance burden, with tighter monitoring, verification, and reporting standards.»

*Analytical inference:* a producer or carrier under the scheme will hold more verified emissions data, which a client may ask a forwarder to carry in shipment documents; the captures state no such request.

## 11. Operational System Requirements

MONITORING: the captures require no system build by a freight business. A customer-reporting lead adds one line to the data requests sent to China-based manufacturers and carriers, once the supporting policies are published, asking whether the supplier is a covered entity and holds a verified emissions report. The capture advises covered firms: «Foreign companies should prepare by strengthening internal carbon management systems and ensuring readiness to meet China’s evolving requirements».

*Analytical inference:* the line lets the business answer a client who asks whether a Chinese supplier's cost base will change; the captures state no right for a forwarder to demand the data.

   "body": "## 1. Purpose and Scope of This Document

This brief covers the European Commission proposal to revise the road vehicle weights and dimensions directive: «The proposal for a new Weights and Dimensions Directive was published on 11 July 2023.» It amends «Council Directive 96/53/EC of 25 July 1996». The proposal is not yet law. The captured status is «Status: Tabled», and the latest captured step is «Trilogue meetings started on 9 December 2025.» The status page reads «As of 22/05/2026», so later steps are not in the captures. Its reach is the Union: «This Directive is addressed to the Member States.» What the text states is quoted between guillemets; what it means for a freight operator is marked *Analytical inference:* and each point for counsel is marked *Legal Confirmation Required:*.

*Analytical inference:* because the proposal is still in negotiation, the figures below are the Commission's, the Parliament's and the Council's positions, and none is final.

## 2. What This Regulation Is and Why It Applies to the Workspace

The directive sets the largest weights and sizes a lorry may have on EU roads. The proposal changes it to reward cleaner trucks: «It provides for new incentives for using low-emission lorries by allowing additional weight for vehicles using zero-emission technologies, as they tend to increase a vehicle's weight.» It also helps intermodal moves: «To encourage intermodal transport, whereby goods are moved using two or more transport modes, lorries, trailers and semitrailers carrying out these operations will be allowed to carry some extra weight.» It also adds height for container moves: «Extra height allowances will also facilitate the transport of high-cube containers by standard vehicles.»

The Commission's own impact summary gives the size of the weight change: «raising the weight limit for zero-emission HDVs from maximum 42 tonnes at present (considered insufficient to compensate for the weight of some of the current zero-emission technology) to 44 tonnes, irrespective of the weight of the zero-emission technology». The proposal enters into force as follows: «This Directive shall enter into force on the twentieth day following that of its publication in the»

The Commission's impact assessment sets the size of the gain and the cost: «the total benefits, which vary between the options from EUR 20 billion (PO-A), EUR 80.2 billion (PO-B) to EUR 97 billion (PO-C), outweigh the total costs ranging from EUR 1.9 billion (PO-A), through EUR 6.5 billion (PO-B) to EUR 15.1 billion (PO-C)».

*Analytical inference:* a road-freight business that runs zero-emission trucks or books intermodal road legs would gain payload or height; one that runs diesel trucks across borders faces the phase-out described below.

## 3. Issues Requiring Immediate Action

MONITORING: the text is a proposal, so no duty falls on a freight business in the next 30 days. A road-freight pricing lead, for each quote that uses a zero-emission truck on a cross-border lane, keeps two payload cases, one at today's limits and one with the extra weight, and prices only the first until a final text is published. An intermodal desk checks whether it is the shipper or the undertaking that organises the move, because the proposal puts a data duty on them: «the shipper or, if different from the shipper, the undertaking which organises the intermodal transport operation, shall ensure that the documents referred to under Articles 3 and 7 of Directive 92/106/ECC, as appropriate, are recorded and made available on an eFTI platform in accordance with Regulation (EU) 2020/1056».

*Analytical inference:* the two-case pricing rests on the open positions of Parliament and Council described below; the second step rests on the Article 6(7) sentence above, which names the shipper or, if different, the undertaking which organises the operation. *Legal Confirmation Required:* whether a freight forwarder that books and sequences an intermodal move is the undertaking which organises the intermodal transport operation.

## 4. How the Workspace Sits in the Compliance Chain

The proposal addresses Member States: «This Directive is addressed to the Member States.» It names the Commission, manufacturers, road operators, the undertaking which organises an intermodal transport operation and shippers. Manufacturers' documentation fixes the extra weight of alternatively fuelled vehicles other than zero-emission vehicles: «The additional weight required by alternatively fuelled vehicles other than zero-emission vehicles shall be defined on the basis of the documentation provided by the manufacturer when the vehicle in question is approved.» It likewise fixes the extra length of zero-emission vehicles: «The additional length required by zero-emission vehicles shall be defined on the basis of the documentation provided by the manufacturer when the vehicle in question is approved.» The consultation list shows the groups heard: «road infrastructure authorities, road transport firms, business associations, shippers, forwarders, Member State national authorities, HDV manufacturers and original equipment manufacturers».

*Analytical inference:* forwarders were consulted but the operative articles quoted here place duties on Member States, on manufacturers and, for data, on the shipper or the undertaking which organises the intermodal operation. A forwarder is bound only where it acts as that undertaking or operates the vehicles itself. *Legal Confirmation Required:* the role a forwarder holds for each type of move.

## 6. Anticipated Authoritative Guidance and Pending Regulatory Events

The next step is the negotiation between Parliament and Council. The Parliament's position: «The Parliament report proposes to increase the maximum weight of zero-emission trucks by four tonnes, to compensate the space and weight needed to fit battery or hydrogen cells, and to provide additional loading capacity.» The Council's position: «ZEVs may receive a weight bonus to account for heavier technology, with different allowances for 5-axle and 6-axle vehicles to protect infrastructure. They may also be up to 0.9 m longer to make room for zero-emission equipment.» The Council's position also covers cross-border intermodal moves: «zero-emission vehicles or vehicle combinations involved in intermodal transport may cross borders even if they exceed directive weight limits, as long as they remain within the limits permitted in both countries.» On «15th January 2026» a trade group urged a quick close, a position stated then, and the captures do not show whether it was met: «We urge the negotiating teams to reach a swift agreement and conclude the trialogues under the Cypriot Presidency.»

A related regulation sets a review that the record dates: «assess, in 2027, the feasibility of a mechanism to adjust the manufacturer’s average specific CO 2 emissions as of 2030». The record stores that review at 1 January 2027, the first day of the year; it is not a step of this directive revision.

*Analytical inference:* the weight figure for a zero-emission truck is open between the Parliament's four tonnes and the Council's separate allowances for 5-axle and 6-axle vehicles, so a quote that needs a firm payload figure must wait for the final text. The captures state no date for agreement.

## 7. Threshold Questions

The length allowance has a fixed cap in the Commission proposal: «The maximum lengths laid down in point 1.1 of Annex I for zero-emission vehicles or vehicle combinations» may be exceeded, as the proposal puts it, «with a maximum of 90 cm, to allow the addition of such devices». A trade group records that the Parliament proposed to widen it: «We support the expansion of the 0.90-meter extension for articulated ZEVs to an unlimited length derogation, provided this does not compromise interoperability with intermodal terminal or rail operations, and as long as the turning circle requirement is met, as proposed by the European Parliament».

*Analytical inference:* the length limit, like the weight limit, is open until Parliament and Council agree. *Legal Confirmation Required:* whether a particular tractor and trailer combination counts as a zero-emission vehicle combination under the final definition.

## 8. Substantive Requirements

Cross-border heavier lorries. «it may not reject or prohibit the use in its territory in international traffic of those vehicle combinations complying with the weight values set for the national transport of goods, provided that such vehicle combinations do not have a maximum authorised weight exceeding 44 tonnes.»

Intermodal exception to that limit. «the 44 tonnes-weight limit set out in paragraph 1 may be exceeded in case the Member State allows higher weight values to those vehicle combinations when involved in an intermodal transport operation.»

Time limit on the cross-border rule. «In view of the expected increase in the uptake of zero-emission vehicles, this Article shall apply until 31 December 2034.»

Zero-emission length. «with a maximum of 90 cm, to allow the addition of such devices».

Intermodal containers. «may be exceeded by 15 cm for vehicles or vehicle combinations engaged in the transport of 45-foot containers or 45-foot swap bodies, empty or loaded, provided that the road transport of the container or swap body in question is part of an intermodal transport operation».

High-cube containers. «the maximum height of vehicles or vehicle combinations that carry containers with a standard external height of 9’6’’ft (high cube containers) is increased to further facilitate the development of intermodal transport».

European Modular Systems. «Member States may allow the circulation in their territories in national and international traffic of European Modular Systems subject to all of the following conditions:»

Enforcement. «Each Member State shall carry out each calendar year at least six checks per one million vehicle-kilometres travelled by vehicles or vehicle combinations used for the transport of goods and falling within the scope of this Directive».

Crisis relief. «Members States may grant temporary exceptions from the application of the weights and dimensions limits set out in Annex I for vehicles used in national traffic, for a period not exceeding two months.»

Transposition. «Member States shall adopt and publish, by [date-of-adoption+2 years] at the latest, the laws, regulations and administrative provisions necessary to comply with this Directive.»

Penalty. The proposal sets no penalty amount; penalties are left to national law.

*Analytical inference:* every rule above falls on a Member State, a manufacturer or an operator of the vehicle, the party each span names; the phase-out means a diesel truck at 44 tonnes crossing a border loses that route once the Article stops applying. No phase-in is stated in Articles 4b and 10b.

*Legal Confirmation Required:* whether a forwarder that subcontracts road legs carries any duty under the weight and enforcement rules, or only the operator of the vehicle does.

Obligations surveyed: 10; workspace-adjacent: 5; extracted as FACT: 10.

## 10. Registration and Reporting Obligations

Member States report to the Commission and the Commission reports back: «The Commission shall analyse the information received pursuant to paragraph 1, and on the basis of the information received, present a report to the European Parliament and the Council on the implementation of this Directive, no later than 13 months after receiving the information from all Member States.» Each vehicle carries proof of its weights: «That additional weight shall be indicated in the official proof required in accordance with Article 6.» Intermodal data go on the electronic platform named in section 3.

*Analytical inference:* the reporting duties fall on Member States and the Commission; the freight business meets them only through the proof of compliance carried on the vehicle and, as the undertaking which organises the move, the platform data.

## 11. Operational System Requirements

MONITORING: nothing in the proposal requires a system build by a freight business today. A digital-freight lead, before the final text is published, checks whether the business's transport management system can issue the carriage data of an intermodal move to an electronic freight transport information platform, because the proposal says «Such information shall be accessible to competent authorities».

*Analytical inference:* the check protects against being unable to produce data on the day the duty applies; the proposal states no start date for it other than entry into force and transposition.

## 13. Adjacent Industry Research and Alternatives

An industry body and a European platform for electric mobility disagree on how far the cross-border rule should reach. The road transport body says «the plenary confirmed the Commission’s proposed 2034 phase-out date, after which the 44-tonne cross-border facilitation measure will only apply to operators with zero-emission vehicles. This approach is not technology neutral.» The electric mobility platform says «the Platform for Electromobility calls on co-legislators to ensure that this file serves as a powerful accelerator for the transition to zero-emission transport of goods» and warns «risking a significant reverse modal shift». Both are industry body views, separate from the proposal.

   "body": "## 1. What's Moving and What Triggered It

COST ALERT: this item follows the shipping carbon cost rules that the Maritime Carbon Intelligence site covers. Its own page holds a contact address, «Pine House, The Square Cheltenham GL54 2LT United Kingdom», and the site sections «Home CCS Regulations Webinars Fuels CO2 shipping Carbon markets Sustainability Finance Technology Insurance Ports and harbours», with no price and no date, so the movement comes from the other sources held for it. Signal event: the Marine Environment Protection Committee of the International Maritime Organization (IMO) «ended with a decision to delay the vote on the adoption of the Net-Zero Framework by one year». The framework it delayed is described by the IMO under the headline «11 April 2025 IMO approves net-zero regulations for global shipping»: «The IMO Net-zero Framework is the first in the world to combine mandatory emissions limits and GHG pricing across an entire industry sector.» The EU side is already running: «Since January 2024, the EU's Emissions Trading System (EU ETS) has been extended to cover CO 2 emissions from all large ships (of 5 000 gross tonnage and above) entering EU ports, regardless of the flag they fly.»

*Analytical inference:* two rule sets are moving shipping carbon cost on different clocks. The EU allowance schedule is fixed and rising, while the start of the global framework is open, so the EU rules are the ones now running on shipping companies, which the Commission page names as the parties that purchase and surrender allowances, and the global rules are a later and uncertain addition; the sources place no cost on a forwarder. The sources hold no price series for either, so no price trajectory is drawn.

## 2. Who's Driving It and What They Want

The delay was political: «This decision followed a contentious meeting that featured political pressure from opponents of adoption.» Since then «some countries have put forward proposals to reopen the regulatory text agreed upon last year at MEPC 83». The Carbon Market Watch group wants the opposite outcome and writes that «it is essential that IMO member states vote in favour of the deal». The Commission's own page frames the EU rules as one half of the picture, with the global measures desirable for the rest of international shipping. Shipping companies are described by a vendor's press release, which is a commercial view: «With global rules still fragmented, owners and charterers will focus on managing exposure rather than long-term transformation.» The same vendor says «regulation running ahead of infrastructure and fuel availability. That gap is what owners are being forced to manage.»

*Analytical inference:* the named parties are IMO Member States, opponents and supporters of adoption, the Commission as legislator of the EU rules and shipping owners and charterers as the cost bearers; a forwarder is not named, so its interest is not stated.

## 3. Expected Trajectory and Conversion Triggers

Conversion trigger: «The session is set to reconvene in the fall of 2026, prolonging policy uncertainty around the transition to zero-emission shipping.» The IMO had planned differently in 2025: «October 2025 (MEPC/ES.2) : Adoption of the amendments during an extraordinary session of the Marine Environment Protection Committee.» and «2027 : Expected entry into force, 16 months after adoption (in accordance with MARPOL articles).» The EU rules were set earlier: «These rules were adopted on 16 May 2023 and entered into force on 5 June 2023.» The first surrender followed: «The first surrendering deadline falls due in September 2025 in all Member States, in respect of emissions reported as taking place from 1 January 2024 to 31 December 2024.» The later view of the Global Maritime Forum gives two ends: «At one extreme, the NZF could be adopted ‘as is’ later this year, entering into force in 2028 and coming into effect in 2029.» and «At the other extreme, a prolonged political deadlock could delay regulatory certainty on GHG reductions for several years.»

- 5 June 2023: the EU rules that bring shipping into the EU Emissions Trading System enter into force
- 1 January 2024: monitoring extends to nitrous oxide and methane emissions for large ships
- 11 April 2025: the IMO approves the Net-Zero Framework at its 83rd session
- September 2025: first allowance surrender deadline under the EU rules
- October 2025: the IMO extraordinary session adjourns without adopting the framework
- 2026: shipping companies surrender allowances for 70% of their emissions reported in 2025
- 2027: shipping companies surrender allowances for 100% of their reported emissions
- 2028: the Net-Zero Framework's Z factors start, if the scheme begins then

*Analytical inference:* the session in the fall of 2026 has now fallen due, but the sources held were written before it and state no result, so the entry into force of the global framework is open between the dates the IMO gave in 2025 and the scenarios of 2026. The EU steps do not wait for it.

## 4. Operational and Cost Implications If It Materializes

EU allowance cost steps up on a schedule the EU states: «2025: for 40% of their emissions reported in 2024; 2026: for 70% of their emissions reported in 2025; 2027 onwards: for 100% of their reported emissions.» The duty sits on the shipping company: «In practice, shipping companies have to purchase and surrender (use) EU ETS emission allowances for each tonne of reported CO 2 (or CO 2 equivalent) emissions in the scope of the EU ETS system.» Coverage depends on the voyage: «100% of emissions that occur between two EU ports and when ships are within EU ports.» and «50% of emissions from voyages starting or ending outside of the EU (allowing the third country to decide on appropriate action for the remaining share of emissions);» From 2026 more gases count: «The EU ETS covers CO 2 (carbon dioxide), CH 4 (methane) and N 2 O (nitrous oxide) emissions, but the two latter only as from 2026.» Monitoring comes first: «Since 1 January 2018, large ships over 5 000 gross tonnage loading or unloading cargo or passengers at ports in the European Economic Area (EEA) must monitor and report related GHG emissions (currently only CO 2 emissions, but also nitrous oxide and methane emissions as of 1 January 2024) and other relevant information.»

The global framework would add a fuel standard and a price on the gap. The IMO says it will be «will become mandatory for large ocean-going ships over 5,000 gross tonnage, which emit 85% of the total CO 2 emissions from international shipping.» Carbon Market Watch gives the price levels the scheme sets and then qualifies them: «which carry a carbon price of $100/tCO2eq.» for the lower level and «priced higher at $380 per tonne of CO2 equivalent.» for the higher level; «However, as discussed below, the actual price levels of these remedial and surplus units (RUs and SUs) are far lower in practice.» Its schedule is short: «Z factors are currently defined for each year from 2028, when the scheme is set to begin, to 2035 only.» The EU already has a comparable standard: «FuelEU Maritime is already in effect. FuelEU introduces GHG intensity thresholds, reward factors, and penalties.» Carbon Market Watch compares the two: «It is a command-and-control type of policy that operates through standards and penalties, comparable in its functioning to the EU’s FuelEU Regulation .» If the framework is adopted as is, «At one extreme, the NZF could be adopted ‘as is’ later this year, entering into force in 2028 and coming into effect in 2029.» Several parts are drafted: «Several guidelines, including zero- and near-zero fuel rewards, a global fuel standard, and fuel pathway certification, have made significant progress, with draft texts now on the table.» The fund is not: «A global climate fund specifically for international shipping (currently referred to as the Net-Zero Fund) remains one of the least developed elements.»

*Analytical inference:* an EU-touching ocean leg carries an allowance cost set by the share of reported emissions surrendered (40%, then 70%, then 100%), so the same voyage costs the shipping company more each step; the global framework would add a second, separate charge on ships over 5,000 gross tonnage. The sources state no surcharge and no pass-through of either cost to cargo owners or forwarders, so the size of any rate effect is open. Corridor identity: the sources describe coverage by voyage type and ship size and name no origin-destination port pair, so the signal is tied to no single lane. The effect by cargo vertical is not stated.

## 5. Competitive Implications

*No content for this section as of November 2026: the sources name no competitor and no position of a freight operator.*

## 6. Client Conversation Talking Points

- Say that the global shipping framework was approved in April 2025 and its vote was delayed by one year: «ended with a decision to delay the vote on the adoption of the Net-Zero Framework by one year».
- Say that the EU allowance cost is rising by a published schedule: «2025: for 40% of their emissions reported in 2024; 2026: for 70% of their emissions reported in 2025; 2027 onwards: for 100% of their reported emissions.»
- Say that the EU already runs a fuel standard on ships: «FuelEU Maritime is already in effect. FuelEU introduces GHG intensity thresholds, reward factors, and penalties.»
- Ask the client whether its contract fixes a shipping surcharge to a date before the fall 2026 session or after, since the result of that session is not held here.

## 7. What the Workspace Should Do Now

Action now: COST ALERT: A carrier-relations lead, at the next rate review, asks each shipping company on EU-touching ocean legs which share of its reported emissions it assumes in its allowance cost (70% for emissions reported in 2025, 100% from 2027) and whether any charge for it is shown as a separate line on the rate.

- A contract lead adds, at the next ocean contract renewal, a clause that lets either side reopen a carbon-related charge when the IMO decides on the Net-Zero Framework, so the result of the fall 2026 session does not leave the charge unchanged by default.
- A pricing lead records, per ocean quote touching an EU port, the date of the quote and whether the rate includes an allowance charge, so the 2027 step to 100% can be priced from the quote history.

*Analytical inference:* the three steps rest on the EU schedule and on the open global vote; the sources state no obligation on a forwarder. *Legal Confirmation Required:* whether a contract that fixes an ocean rate allows the shipping company to add an allowance or fuel standard charge during its term.

   "body": "## 1. Purpose and Scope of This Document

This document covers «DIRECTIVE (EU) 2022/362 OF THE EUROPEAN PARLIAMENT AND OF THE COUNCIL of 24 February 2022 amending Directives 1999/62/EC, 1999/37/EC and (EU) 2019/520, as regards the charging of vehicles for the use of certain infrastructures». Where this directive applies: the Member States of the Union, because «This Directive is addressed to the Member States.» Its Article 1 replaces and inserts articles in Directive 1999/62/EC, the road charging directive, and the article numbers in the quotations below, such as 7ca and 7ga, are those of that Directive as this one amends it. What the Directive says is stated from its own text; what it means for a freight business is marked *Analytical inference:* and each point for counsel is marked *Legal Confirmation Required:*.

## 2. What This Regulation Is and Why It Applies to the Workspace

The Directive sets the rules Member States follow when they charge lorries and other vehicles for using roads. It covers two kinds of charge: «This Directive applies to: (a) vehicle taxes imposed on heavy goods vehicles; (b) tolls and user charges imposed on vehicles.» A toll is distance-based: «“toll” means a specified amount payable in respect of a vehicle based on the distance travelled on a given infrastructure and on the type of the vehicle» A user charge is time-based: «“user charge” means a specified amount payment of which confers the right for a vehicle to use for a given period the infrastructures» The Directive follows the principle Parliament and Council state: «to move towards the full application of the ‘polluter pays’ and ‘user pays’ principles»

The directive enters into force as Article 5 says: «This Directive shall enter into force on the twentieth day following that of its publication in the Official Journal of the European Union .» The text itself counts several periods from 24 March 2022.

The Directive treats heavy goods vehicles as heavy-duty vehicles: «“heavy-duty vehicle” means a vehicle with a technically permissible maximum laden mass exceeding 3,5 tonnes» Its transport operator is defined as «“transport operator” means any undertaking transporting goods or passengers by road»

*Analytical inference:* heavy goods vehicles on EU roads are the freight activity closest to the Directive. The Directive requires its changes of Member States and states no pass-through of a toll or user charge to a forwarder or its client, so the effect on a quote depends on each transport operator's own terms.

## 3. Issues Requiring Immediate Action

COST ALERT: a new cost element is already in force on tolled roads. «From 25 March 2026, Member States shall apply an external-cost charge for traffic-based air pollution to heavy-duty vehicles on the tolled network referred to in Article 7(1).» Member States may leave it out in one case: «Member States may decide not to apply an external-cost charge on those road sections where this would lead to the diversion of the most polluting vehicles, resulting in negative impacts on road safety and public health.» The next fixed date is the end of time-based charges on the main network: «From 25 March 2030, Member States shall not apply user charges for heavy-duty vehicles on the core trans-European transport network.»

- A pricing lead, at the next EU road tariff review, splits the toll line of each EU road leg by charge type (a distance-based toll or a time-based user charge) and by the Member State that levies it, so that the end of user charges on the core network on 25 March 2030 can be priced leg by leg.
- A carrier-relations lead asks each road transport operator on EU legs, before the next rate review, which CO2 emission class each vehicle is in and whether the quoted toll line already carries the air pollution charge.

*Analytical inference:* both steps rest on the quoted Articles, which place the duty on Member States and not on a forwarder. *Legal Confirmation Required:* whether a road haulage contract lets the transport operator pass a toll change on to the forwarder or its client, and under which clause.

## 4. How the Workspace Sits in the Compliance Chain

The Directive is addressed to the Member States and names the Commission, the road user, the driver and the transport operator. Tolls must not discriminate: «Tolls and user charges shall not discriminate, directly or indirectly, on the grounds of: (a) the nationality of the road user; (b) the Member State or the third country of establishment of the transport operator;» The transport operator appears in the evidence rule: «Where a driver or, if appropriate, the transport operator or the European Electronic Toll Service (EETS) provider, is unable to provide evidence of the emission class of the vehicle for the purposes of Article 7g(2), Article 7ga or Article 7gb, Member States may apply tolls or user charges up to the highest level chargeable.» A forwarder, shipper or carrier-relations role is not named.

*Analytical inference:* a forwarder meets these charges through the toll lines of the transport operators it books, not through a duty of its own. *Legal Confirmation Required:* which party in a booked road move is the road user or transport operator for a given toll, and whether the contract lets the forwarder see the toll line.

## 6. Anticipated Authoritative Guidance and Pending Regulatory Events

The text sets seven dated steps, some for the Commission and some for Member States. Light vehicles (Commission): «By 25 March 2027, the Commission shall assess the implementation and effectiveness of this Directive with regard to the charging of light-duty vehicles.» The carbon price link: «By 25 March 2027, the Commission shall assess the implementation and effectiveness of external-cost charging for CO 2 emissions, as well as its coherence with Directive 2003/87/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council ( * ) and Council Directive 2003/96/EC ( ** ) .» The Commission acts by delegated act only if two conditions both hold: this Article has not been amended by 1 January 2027, and Directive 2003/87/EC or Directive 2003/96/EC has been amended so that at least part of the external costs of CO2 emissions from road transport is effectively internalised. The text: «In the event that this Article has not been amended accordingly by 1 January 2027 but Directive 2003/87/EC or Directive 2003/96/EC has been amended in a manner resulting in an effective internalisation of at least part of the external costs of CO 2 emissions from road transport, the Commission shall adopt delegated acts in accordance with Article 9d of this Directive, amending Annex IIIc to this Directive to adjust the reference values of the external-cost charge for CO 2 emissions, taking into account the effective carbon price applied to road transport fuels in the Union.» The power for such acts runs for a fixed period: «The power to adopt delegated acts referred to in Article 9d shall be conferred on the Commission for a period of five years from 24 March 2022.» A look at the maximum user charge rates is also due: «The Commission shall, every five years, after 24 March 2022, review the maximum rates for the user charges in Annex II» Member State reporting repeats: «By 25 March 2025, and every five years thereafter, Member States shall make public in aggregate form a report on tolls and user charges levied on their territory.» Common systems have a later end: «Where Member States apply a common system for user charges in accordance with Article 8, those Member States shall adapt or discontinue the common system by 25 March 2032.»

*Analytical inference:* the 25 March 2027 assessments are the point at which the Commission decides whether to propose changes to the carbon element of tolls and to light vehicle charging, and the 1 January 2027 date in the delegated-act clause comes first, but that clause applies only if both conditions above are met. The next Member State report after 25 March 2025 falls on 25 March 2030 on the five-year rhythm in the text. The text states no outcome of any of these steps.

## 7. Threshold Questions

Whether a vehicle is covered turns on its mass: «“heavy-duty vehicle” means a vehicle with a technically permissible maximum laden mass exceeding 3,5 tonnes» Which charge it meets turns on its use: «Member States shall not impose both tolls and user charges on any given category of vehicle for the use of a single road section.» Whether a charge is reduced turns on its CO2 class: «Member States shall establish for each type of heavy-duty vehicle the following CO 2 emission classes:»

*Analytical inference:* the Directive defines a heavy-duty vehicle by mass and does not name a freight vehicle type, so a vehicle at or under that mass is outside these heavy-duty rules. *Legal Confirmation Required:* the class a given vehicle falls in and the Member State toll that applies to it.

## 8. Substantive Requirements

Scope. «This Directive applies to: (a) vehicle taxes imposed on heavy goods vehicles; (b) tolls and user charges imposed on vehicles.»

Time-based charges on the core network. «From 25 March 2030, Member States shall not apply user charges for heavy-duty vehicles on the core trans-European transport network.» «By way of derogation from paragraph 10, Member States may apply user charges for heavy-duty vehicles on sections of the core trans-European transport network but only in duly justified cases»

Air pollution. «From 25 March 2026, Member States shall apply an external-cost charge for traffic-based air pollution to heavy-duty vehicles on the tolled network referred to in Article 7(1).» «The external-cost charge related to traffic-based air pollution shall not apply to heavy-duty vehicles which comply with the most stringent of Euro emission standards.»

CO2 variation. «Member States shall vary infrastructure charges and user charges for heavy-duty vehicles in accordance with this Article.» The reductions against class 1 run from «5 % to 15 % reduction compared to the charge applicable for CO 2 emission class 1» for class 2 up to «50 % to 75 % reduction compared to the charge applicable for CO 2 emission class 1» for class 5, the zero-emission class. «The variations referred to in this Article shall not be designed to generate additional revenues.»

Zero-emission vehicles. «Member States may provide for reduced rates of infrastructure or user charges, or exemptions to pay infrastructure or user charges for zero emission vehicles of any vehicle group from 24 March 2022 until 31 December 2025.» «From 1 January 2026, such reductions shall be limited to 75 % compared to the charge applicable to CO 2 emission class 1, as defined in paragraph 2.»

Vans and minibuses. «From 1 January 2026, where technically practicable, Member States shall vary the tolls and the annual rate of the user charges for vans and minibuses according to the environmental performance of the vehicle, in accordance with the rules set out in Annex VII.»

Higher carbon charges. «Member States may apply higher external-cost charges for CO 2 emissions than the reference values set out in Annex IIIc, provided that this is done in a non-discriminatory manner, and limited to no more than twice the values set out in Annex IIIc.»

Annual amounts. «The amounts in euros laid down in Annex II and the amounts in cents laid down in the Tables of Annexes IIIb and IIIc shall be adapted every two years in order to take account of changes in the EU-wide Harmonised Index of Consumer Prices (HICP) excluding energy and unprocessed food, as published by the Commission (Eurostat).» «The first adaptation shall take place by 31 March 2025.»

Transposition. «Member States shall bring into force the laws, regulations and administrative provisions necessary to comply with this Directive by 25 March 2024.»

The Directive states no penalty, fine or sanction and names no enforcement body.

*Analytical inference:* each duty above falls on a Member State, not on a freight operator, and the reduction ranges are ranges a Member State applies, so a given toll depends on national choices the Directive does not state. The text sets the zero-emission reduction cap at 75 % from 1 January 2026, and the 5 % to 15 % and 50 % to 75 % bands are the reductions against class 1.

*Legal Confirmation Required:* which Member State rules apply to a given road leg and whether any of these duties creates a charge or liability for a forwarder or its client.

## 10. Registration and Reporting Obligations

Member States report in public: «By 25 March 2025, and every five years thereafter, Member States shall make public in aggregate form a report on tolls and user charges levied on their territory.» The report covers, among other items, «(e) the external-cost charge levied for each combination of class of vehicle, type of road and period of time;» and «(l) the evolution of the share vehicles belonging to the various emission classes on tolled roads.» Member States also report to the Commission: «Member States shall communicate to the Commission the text of the main measures of national law which they adopt in the field covered by this Directive.» A Member State that does not vary a toll must say so: «A Member State that decides not to apply Article 7ca(3), Article 7ga(1) and Article 7gb(2) in accordance with the second subparagraph of this paragraph shall notify the Commission of its decision.»

*Analytical inference:* these are Member State duties; the text states no registration or reporting step for a forwarder. The report in aggregate form is where the share of vehicles by emission class on tolled roads becomes public. *Legal Confirmation Required:* whether any national toll registration applies to a forwarder.

## 11. Operational System Requirements

COST ALERT: the Directive asks for no system of a forwarder, but the toll a vehicle pays depends on proof of its emission class: «Where a driver or, if appropriate, the transport operator or the European Electronic Toll Service (EETS) provider, is unable to provide evidence of the emission class of the vehicle for the purposes of Article 7g(2), Article 7ga or Article 7gb, Member States may apply tolls or user charges up to the highest level chargeable.» «Member States shall take the measures necessary to ensure that the road user can declare the emission class of the vehicle at least through electronic means before using the infrastructure.» «Member States may take the measures necessary to ensure that the provision of evidence subsequent to the use of the infrastructure is accepted for 30 days or a longer period»

- A pricing-data owner adds to each EU road leg record a field for the vehicle's CO2 emission class and a field for the Member State toll type, so the charge in a quote can be matched to the reduction the vehicle can claim.
- A carrier-relations lead asks the transport operators on EU legs how they declare the emission class before using the infrastructure, since a missing proof can lead to the highest chargeable level.

*Analytical inference:* the Directive says a Member State may charge the highest level without evidence; it does not say who bears that cost in a booked move. *Legal Confirmation Required:* whether the contract places the cost of a missing emission class declaration on the transport operator or the forwarder.

## 12. Exemptions and Edge Cases

Member States may exempt or reduce: «Member States may provide for reduced tolls or user charges, or exemptions from the obligation to pay tolls or user charges for:» among them «zero-emission vehicles with a technically permissible maximum laden mass up to 4,25 tonnes.» For roads under old concession contracts: «Member States may choose not to apply Article 7ca(3), Article 7g(1) and (2), Article 7ga and Article 7gb to tolls and user charges on those infrastructures until the concession contract is renewed or the tolling or charging arrangement is substantially amended.» A mark-up has a limit: «A mark-up may not be applied on road sections on which a congestion charge is levied.»

*Analytical inference:* a zero-emission vehicle may pay less or nothing, within the caps above, depending on the Member State; a concession road may keep older rules until its contract is renewed. *Legal Confirmation Required:* whether a particular road leg sits under a concession arrangement that keeps the older rules.

   "body": "## 1. Purpose and Scope of This Document

This brief covers «COMMISSION IMPLEMENTING REGULATION (EU) 2025/35 of 13 January 2025 implementing Regulation (EU) 2019/1242 of the European Parliament and of the Council by determining the procedures for the in-service verification of the CO 2 emissions of heavy-duty vehicles». It is an EU regulation: «This Regulation shall be binding in its entirety and directly applicable in all Member States.» It sets how national authorities test lorries and buses already on the road to check the CO2 figures their makers declared. Zero-emission vehicles are outside it: «This Regulation does not apply to zero emission heavy-duty vehicles as defined in Article 3, point (11), of Regulation (EU) 2019/1242.» What the text states is quoted between guillemets; what it means for a freight operator is marked *Analytical inference:* and each point for counsel is marked *Legal Confirmation Required:*.

*Analytical inference:* the Regulation is addressed to type-approval authorities, manufacturers and the Commission; it names no freight forwarder, carrier or shipper, so a freight business meets it only as a buyer or user of the trucks that are tested.

## 2. What This Regulation Is and Why It Applies to the Workspace

The Regulation fills in a procedure that the parent CO2 standards regulation created: «This Regulation defines detailed procedures for the in-service verification of heavy-duty vehicles referred to in Delegated Regulation (EU) 2024/1127.» The Commission explains the aim: «is a new procedure which aims to make sure that the official CO 2 emission values, provided in the vehicles’ customer information files issued by vehicle manufacturers, are correct and correspond to actual emissions when vehicles are on the road.» The Commission also gives the reason it matters: «Lorries, buses and coaches are responsible for over 6% of total EU emissions of CO 2».

It enters into force as follows: «This Regulation shall enter into force on the twentieth day following that of its publication in the» The first test campaign is dated by the Commission: «Beginning from July 2025, each year, national type-approval authorities will test a sample of vehicles that are on the road».

*Analytical inference:* a freight business that buys or leases heavy trucks relies on the CO2 values in the vehicle's customer information file for its own carbon reporting and for client quotes; this Regulation checks those values. The text states no duty on a freight business.

## 3. Issues Requiring Immediate Action

MONITORING: no duty falls on a freight business, and the text states no cost to operators. A fleet-procurement lead, in each tender for heavy trucks, asks the maker whether the offered model's engine, transmission, tyre or air-drag family is on the Commission's annual list of highest-risk families, which the Commission publishes each year: «Each year, by 30 June, the Commission shall publish a report containing a list of VTP families, ISV air drag families, CFD families and ISV tyre families with the highest risk of a deviation in the CO 2 emission values.» The answer goes into the tender file with the date.

*Analytical inference:* the step rests on the risk-list sentence above; it gives the buyer an early sign that a declared CO2 value may later be reported as deviating. The text states no effect on truck prices or on the buyer's own figures.

## 4. How the Workspace Sits in the Compliance Chain

The Regulation names the granting approval authority, the manufacturer, the Commission and the type-approval authorities. The authority that tests is the one that licensed the manufacturer's simulation tool: «type-approval authorities which granted manufacturers a licence to operate a simulation tool under Regulation (EC) No 595/2009 of the European Parliament and of the Council». A manufacturer can contest a result: «the manufacturer may contest the results within 20 working days after receiving the test report». A forwarder, carrier or fleet operator is not named.

*Analytical inference:* a freight business is outside the compliance chain; the manufacturer carries the testing consequence. *Legal Confirmation Required:* whether a buyer's contract with a truck maker gives any right to be told of a deviation found for the model it bought.

## 6. Anticipated Authoritative Guidance and Pending Regulatory Events

The Commission and its research centre have started the annual cycle. The research centre's 2025 risk assessment names the high-risk groups: «Based on the assessment, 35 tyre families, 17 air drag families, 13 engine VTP families, and 4 transmission VTP families have been classified as high risk.» Authorities publish what they found: «Before 30 September of each calendar year, the granting approval authority shall publish an overview of the in-service verifications performed in the previous reporting period and its conclusions issued in that reporting period».

The parent regulation sets 2027 steps that the record dates: «The Commission shall, if appropriate, submit a legislative proposal to that effect by 2027 at the latest.» and «assess, in 2027, the feasibility of a mechanism to adjust the manufacturer’s average specific CO 2 emissions as of 2030». The record stores these 2027 steps of the parent regulation at 1 January 2027, the first day of the year; they are not steps of this Regulation.

*Analytical inference:* each year brings a new risk list by 30 June and a results overview before 30 September; the captures state the dates of the cycle but no results for any manufacturer.

## 7. Threshold Questions

The size of the manufacturer decides which tests apply: «for each manufacturer for whom the ‘total number of vehicles under Article 9 of Regulation (EU) 2017/2400’ is equal to or higher than 5 000, the granting approval authority shall perform each reporting period one mass test per manufacturer and one artificial strategies test per manufacturer». The kind of vehicle decides scope: «This Regulation does not apply to zero emission heavy-duty vehicles as defined in Article 3, point (11), of Regulation (EU) 2019/1242.»

*Analytical inference:* a battery-electric truck is outside the Regulation, so only trucks with combustion engines are tested. *Legal Confirmation Required:* whether a particular vehicle model falls in the zero-emission definition of the parent regulation.

## 8. Substantive Requirements

Scope. «This Regulation does not apply to zero emission heavy-duty vehicles as defined in Article 3, point (11), of Regulation (EU) 2019/1242.»

Test vehicles. «they have a minimum mileage of 25 000 km».

Test report to the manufacturer. «Within 20 working days of finishing the tests, the granting approval authority shall make the test report available to the manufacturer of the vehicles or tyres concerned».

Authority conclusion. «The granting approval authority shall transmit its conclusion to the manufacturer concerned and to the Commission at the latest 40 working days, or in case of extension in accordance with paragraph 2, at the latest 80 working days, after having sent the test report to the manufacturer under paragraph 2.»

Artificial strategies. «artificial strategies shall be understood as any software, control logic, hardware or component on board or relating to the vehicle, which reduces the vehicle’s CO 2 emission or fuel consumption values in the tests performed for the purpose of CO 2 emissions certification, but which does not operate consistently when the vehicle is in-service, taking into account the difference between those test conditions and the in-service conditions, unless that inconsistent operation results from requirements laid down in Union law or is justified by the necessity to protect the vehicle against immediate damage or to ensure the safe operation of the vehicle».

Fallback deviation. «the size of the deviation in the CO 2 emission values shall be 10 % of the CO 2 emission value of the reference CO 2 emissions of the vehicle sub-group».

Correction of the manufacturer's average. «The Commission shall also apply the size of the deviation of the CO 2 emission values to the vehicles concerned, as determined in accordance with Article 22, for correcting the average specific CO 2 emissions of the manufacturer for the ten reporting periods prior to the reporting period of the year in which the conclusion was issued, but not earlier than the reporting period of the year 2025.»

Penalty. This Regulation sets no penalty itself. The parent regulation turns the corrected average into a financial penalty on the manufacturer: «(a) from 2025 to 2029, (Excess CO 2 emissions premium) = (Excess CO 2 emissions × 4 250 EUR/gCO 2 /tkm) (b) from 2030 onwards, (Excess CO 2 emissions premium) = (Excess CO 2 emissions × 6 800 EUR/gCO 2 /tkm).» The premium applies only where excess emissions are found: «Where a manufacturer is found, pursuant to paragraph 2, to have excess CO 2 emissions in a given reporting period from 2025 onwards, the Commission shall impose an excess CO 2 emissions premium». The link from the corrected average is in the parent regulation: «The Commission shall take the deviations referred to in paragraph 1 into account for the purpose of calculating the average specific CO 2 emissions of a manufacturer.»

*Analytical inference:* a corrected average leads to a premium only if the parent regulation's test then finds excess emissions; the sources do not say how often that happens. The duties above fall on approval authorities, manufacturers and the Commission, the party each span names; the penalty falls on the manufacturer, and the captures state no pass-through of it to buyers of trucks. No phase-in is stated in Articles 3 to 23.

*Legal Confirmation Required:* whether any term of a truck purchase or lease lets a maker pass a corrected-average penalty on to the buyer.

Obligations surveyed: 10; workspace-adjacent: 3; extracted as FACT: 10.

## 10. Registration and Reporting Obligations

The authority reports to the manufacturer and to the Commission: «upload it in an encrypted format to a dedicated Commission server». The Commission describes the public side: «National authorities will then publish their findings and report them to the Commission.» Test data stay closed: «The data and parameters specified in points (a) to (e) shall not be published.»

*Analytical inference:* the findings are published by authorities, so a buyer can read which families were tested and concluded on, but not the raw test data.

## 11. Operational System Requirements

MONITORING: the text requires no system build by a freight business. A fleet-carbon lead keeps, for each heavy truck bought or leased, the CO2 value from the customer information file together with the model family and the date of purchase, because the Commission explains: «Should there be deviations, the Commission will recalculate the average specific CO 2 emissions of the concerned manufacturers to check whether they are complying with their emission targets».

*Analytical inference:* the record lets the business show which value it used if a family it bought is later found to deviate; the captures state no change to the figures in a buyer's file.

## 13. Adjacent Industry Research and Alternatives

A clean-transport research group describes the parent standards that the verification supports: «The revised standards maintain the CO 2 reduction target of 15% for 2025 and raise the 2030 target to 45% while introducing a 65% reduction target for 2035 and a 90% target for 2040.» It is an industry body view of the parent regulation, separate from this Regulation.

## 14. Confirmed Regulatory Timeline

- 20 June 2019: the parent regulation is dated, «Regulation (EU) 2019/1242 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 20 June 2019»
- 8 February 2024: the Commission adopts the guiding-principles delegated regulation, «On 8 February 2024, the Commission adopted a»
- 13 January 2025: this Regulation is adopted, «Done at Brussels, 13 January 2025.»
- 14 January 2025: this Regulation is published, «On 14 January 2025, the European Commission published a regulation on the verification of CO 2 emissions from lorries, buses and coaches in service by national authorities.»
- 2025: first reporting period for corrections, «not earlier than the reporting period of the year 2025»
- July 2025: first annual test campaign starts, «Beginning from July 2025, each year, national type-approval authorities will test a sample of vehicles that are on the road»
- 1 July 2025: tyre families concern vehicles registered after this date, «all vehicles registered after 1 July 2025 using tyres from the ISV tyre family concerned»
- 30 June each year: the Commission publishes the high-risk list
