Some batteries are outside the Regulation: «This Regulation does not apply to batteries that are incorporated into or that are specifically designed to be incorporated into: (a) equipment connected with the protection of Member States’ essential security interests, arms, munitions and war material». A very small battery need not carry the symbol: «Where the size of the battery is such that the separate collection symbol would be smaller than 0,47 × 0,47 cm, the battery does not need to be marked with that symbol.» The Commission page records a derogation route for portable batteries inside products: «Article 11(2) of Regulation (EU) 2023/1542 establishes derogations from the removability and replaceability requirements for portable batteries incorporated in products.»

   "body": "## 1. Purpose and Scope of This Document

This document covers the EU Fit for 55 package, the Commission's set of climate proposals. The Commission's page on shipping dates it: «As part of the European Commission’s legislative proposals to deliver the European Green Deal - the ‘Fit for 55’ package - published on 14 July 2021, several proposals addressed maritime transport’s climate impact, in addition to the extension of the EU ETS.» Its aim is the Union's 2030 target: «The ‘Fit for 55’ legislative package aims to implement the 2030 greenhouse gas emissions reduction target.» A package is not one instrument, so this document reads the instruments of it that bear on freight: aviation fuel (ReFuelEU Aviation), shipping (the maritime extension of the EU Emissions Trading System, the monitoring rules and FuelEU Maritime), border carbon pricing (the carbon border adjustment mechanism, CBAM), heavy-duty vehicle CO2 standards and alternative fuels infrastructure. A related file on transport emissions accounting is read beside them. The package communication itself is not among the pages read, so what it says in its own words is not stated here. What each instrument requires is stated from its own text; what it means for a freight business is marked *Analytical inference:* and each point for counsel is marked *Legal Confirmation Required:*. The jurisdiction is the Union.

## 2. What This Regulation Is and Why It Applies to the Workspace

The package works sector by sector, and each part has its own scope. Aviation: «This Regulation applies to aircraft operators, to Union airports and their respective Union airport managing bodies, and to aviation fuel suppliers.» An aircraft operator is defined by volume: «‘aircraft operator’ means a person that operated at least 500 commercial passenger air transport flights, or 52 commercial all-cargo air transport flights departing from Union airports in the previous reporting period». Shipping: «This Regulation applies to all ships of above 5 000 gross tonnage that serve the purpose of transporting passengers or cargo for commercial purposes, regardless of their flag». The trading system reaches ships too: «Since January 2024, the EU's Emissions Trading System (EU ETS) has been extended to cover CO 2 emissions from all large ships (of 5 000 gross tonnage and above) entering EU ports, regardless of the flag they fly.» The rules took effect as the Commission states: «These rules were adopted on 16 May 2023 and entered into force on 5 June 2023.» Imports: «This Regulation applies to goods listed in Annex I originating in a third country, where those goods, or processed products from those goods resulting from the inward processing procedure referred to in Article 256 of Regulation (EU) No 952/2013, are imported into the customs territory of the Union.» Road, against a 2019 baseline: «compared to the average CO 2 emissions of the reporting period of the year 2019»: «(b) 45 % for all vehicle sub-groups other than vocational vehicles for the reporting periods of the years 2030 to 2034; (c) 65 % for all vehicle sub-groups for the reporting periods of the years 2035 to 2039; (d) 90 % for all vehicle sub-groups for the reporting periods of the year 2040 onwards.» Infrastructure: «Revising the Directive on Deployment of Alternative Fuels Infrastructure , which would set, among other benefits, mandatory targets for shore-side electricity supply at maritime and inland waterway ports».

*Analytical inference:* the duties named in these passages fall on aircraft operators, aviation fuel suppliers, ship companies, importers, vehicle manufacturers and infrastructure operators, not on a freight business as such. A freight business meets the package through the cost and data its carriers and customs routes pass on, and directly where it imports or acts as customs representative. *Legal Confirmation Required:* which of these roles, if any, a freight business holds for a given consignment.

## 3. Issues Requiring Immediate Action

COST ALERT: the dated steps below set costs and duties for ship companies, fuel suppliers and importers; the texts state no pass-through of them to freight rates. The closest dated duty in the texts read is for charging infrastructure: «From 1 January 2027, operators of recharging points shall ensure that all publicly accessible recharging points operated by them, with a power output equal to or more than 50 kW deployed along the TEN-T road network or deployed on a safe and secure parking area, including recharging points deployed before 13 April 2024, comply with the requirements set out in points (a) or (b).». For importers the next step is the border carbon declaration. The original text of the CBAM Regulation says: «The first CBAM declaration, in respect of the calendar year 2026, should be submitted by 31 May 2027.» The Commission's CBAM page lists «Regulation (EU) 2025/2083 as regards simplifying and strengthening the CBAM», so that date is superseded; the amended date is not among the pages held. The surrender share for ship companies rises in steps: «2025: for 40% of their emissions reported in 2024; 2026: for 70% of their emissions reported in 2025; 2027 onwards: for 100% of their reported emissions.»

- A customs lead lists, before the first declaration falls due, each client import of goods in the border mechanism's goods list and records who the importer is, and whether that importer has applied: «Goods shall be imported into the customs territory of the Union only by an authorised CBAM declarant.»
- A carrier-relations lead asks each shipping line and air carrier in writing, at the next rate review, whether the cost of trading system allowances, of the FuelEU penalty or of sustainable aviation fuel is added to the rate, and how it is calculated.
- A pricing lead records, per quote that includes a sea leg into or out of the Union, whether the rate includes a trading system or fuel regulation charge, so the cost step to 100 percent of reported emissions from 2027 can be priced.

*Analytical inference:* the first action rests on the importer rule and the declaration date above, which the amending Regulation supersedes, the other two on the stated shares for shipping emissions; none of the passages read states how a carrier passes these costs to a customer, so the second and third actions test that gap rather than assume a surcharge. *Legal Confirmation Required:* whether the business or its client is the importer or the customs representative for each border mechanism import.

## 4. How the Workspace Sits in the Compliance Chain

Each instrument names its own parties. Shipping: «‘company’ means the shipowner or any other organisation or person such as the manager or the bareboat charterer, which has assumed the responsibility for the operation of the ship from the shipowner». Aviation suppliers: «aviation fuel suppliers shall ensure that all aviation fuel made available to aircraft operators at each Union airport contains the minimum shares of SAF». Imports: «Where such an importer appoints an indirect customs representative in accordance with Article 18 of Regulation (EU) No 952/2013 and the indirect customs representative agrees to act as an authorised CBAM declarant, the indirect customs representative shall submit the application for an authorisation.». During the transition: «Where the importer is not established in a Member State, the reporting obligations shall apply to the indirect customs representative.» Emissions accounting, as the Commission proposed it: «This Regulation applies to any entity providing or organising freight and passenger services in the Union that calculates greenhouse gas emissions of a transport service starting or ending on the Union territory and discloses disaggregated information on those emissions to any third party for commercial or regulatory purposes.» and as agreed: «The regulation will apply to companies that choose to publish emissions from their activities.»

*Analytical inference:* a freight business that organises transport sits beside the ship company and aircraft operator, which carry the allowance and fuel duties, and takes the cost through rates; where it acts as indirect customs representative, the border mechanism passes reporting duties to it. The accounting regulation reaches an organiser of freight only if it publishes emissions. *Legal Confirmation Required:* whether the business is an indirect customs representative or an organiser of freight services under these definitions, and which party is the importer of each consignment.

## 5. Authoritative Guidance Document Analysis

The Commission's shipping page lists the acts that carry out the trading system rules for ships, among them «Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2023/2297 of 26 October 2023 identifying neighbouring container transhipment ports pursuant to Directive 2003/87/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council» and «Commission Implementing Decision (EU) 2024/411 of 30 January 2024 on the list of shipping companies specifying the administering authority in respect of a shipping company in accordance with Directive 2003/87/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council». The aviation regulator's page states: «The Regulation applies from 1 January 2024 and its first reporting obligation (Article 8) for aircraft operators is expected in 2025.»

*Analytical inference:* these acts set which ports count as neighbouring transhipment ports and which authority administers each shipping company, so they decide where a ship's allowance duty is administered; none of the passages read states a rule for forwarders. *Legal Confirmation Required:* whether a transhipment of a client's container at a neighbouring port changes which share of a voyage's emissions is covered.

## 6. Anticipated Authoritative Guidance and Pending Regulatory Events

The texts read set Commission and Member State steps with dates, and the accounting regulation is still to be adopted. «Following the political agreement, the European Parliament and the Council will now formally adopt the regulation, which will enter into force 20 days after publication in the Official Journal of the EU.» «The regulation’s provisions will be implemented 48 months after entry into force.» Other dated steps: «By 1 January 2027, and every four years thereafter, the Commission shall present a report to the European Parliament»; «By 25 September 2026, and every five years thereafter, Member States shall make public a report on the» (that date has passed and the pages do not say whether the report was made); «By 31 December 2026 and every five years thereafter, the Commission should carry out a review of this Regulation.» «By 30 June 2027, the Commission shall submit to the European Parliament and to the Council a report».

   "body": "## 1. Purpose and Scope of This Document

This document covers the amending Regulation that changes the EU carbon border adjustment mechanism (CBAM): «On 17 October 2025, Regulation (EU) 2025/2083 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 8 October 2025 amending Regulation (EU) 2023/956 as regards simplifying and strengthening the carbon border adjustment mechanism ("CBAM") was published in the Official Journal of the European Union». Why it was made: «the Commission has been collecting data and information on the implementation of the carbon border adjustment mechanism (the ‘CBAM’) as provided for therein». Its reach: «This Regulation shall be binding in its entirety and directly applicable in all Member States.» What the Regulation requires is stated from its own text; what it means for a freight business is marked *Analytical inference:* and each point for counsel is marked *Legal Confirmation Required:*. The pages are read as captured.

## 2. What This Regulation Is and Why It Applies to the Workspace

It amends the CBAM Regulation to ease small importers and tighten the mechanism. It took effect as ICAP, a carbon market news page, reports: «On 20 October 2025, the amendments to the EU Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) took effect.» The law sets the start: «This Regulation shall enter into force on the third day following that of its publication in the Official Journal of the European Union .»

The small importer exemption: «A new threshold based on cumulative net mass of the imported goods in a given calendar year per importer (the ‘single mass-based threshold’) should be introduced in Regulation (EU) 2023/956, and initially be set at a level of 50 tonnes.» Who counts as the importer is redrawn: «‘(15) “importer” means either the person lodging a customs declaration for release for free circulation of goods or a bill of discharge in accordance with Article 175(5) of Delegated Regulation (EU) 2015/2446 in its own name and on its own behalf or, where the customs declaration is lodged by an indirect customs representative in accordance with Article 18 of Regulation (EU) No 952/2013, the person on whose behalf such a declaration is lodged;»

*Analytical inference:* an indirect customs representative is the person who lodges the customs declaration on behalf of an importer, so a freight business that lodges import declarations for clients can fall in the Regulation's chain without being the importer. *Legal Confirmation Required:* whether the business lodges declarations as an indirect customs representative for goods in the mechanism's scope.

## 3. Issues Requiring Immediate Action

COST ALERT: certificate cost starts to fall on declarants, with quarterly holding from 1 January 2027. The closest dated step is «‘(c) Article 22(2) shall apply from 1 January 2027; (d) Article 20(1), (3), (4) and (5) shall apply from 1 February 2027.’» The duty it starts: «From 2027, the authorised CBAM declarant shall ensure that the number of CBAM certificates on its account in the CBAM registry at the end of each quarter corresponds to at least 50 % of the embedded emissions in all goods it has imported since the beginning of the calendar year». The first declaration and surrender: «By 30 September of each year, and for the first time in 2027 for the year 2026, the authorised CBAM declarant shall surrender via the CBAM registry a number of CBAM certificates»

- A customs lead lists, before 1 January 2027, each client for which the business lodges import declarations and confirms for each whether the business must hold declarant status: «An indirect customs representative shall obtain the status of authorised CBAM declarant prior to importing goods into the customs territory of the Union.»
- A finance lead sets, before the first quarter end of 2027, the certificate cash and the holding level for each declarant account and prices it against the rule: «The Commission shall calculate the price of CBAM certificates as the average of the closing prices of EU ETS allowances on the auction platform».
- A contract lead adds, at the next client renewal, a clause that states who is the importer, who pays for certificates and who answers for the declaration, because «Where an indirect customs representative acts as an authorised CBAM declarant on behalf of an importer, the indirect customs representative shall be subject to the obligations applicable to the importer pursuant to this Regulation».

*Analytical inference:* the three actions rest on the representative's duty as declarant, the quarterly holding rule and the price rule above; the text states no right of the representative to recover the cost from the client, so the clause fixes that. *Legal Confirmation Required:* whether a given client arrangement makes the business the declarant for that client's imports.

## 4. How the Workspace Sits in the Compliance Chain

The Regulation names an importer, an indirect customs representative and an authorised declarant. An importer in a Member State applies in its own right: «Any importer established in a Member State shall, prior to importing goods into the customs territory of the Union, apply for the status of authorised CBAM declarant». Where the importer is not in a Member State: «Where an importer is not established in a Member State, the indirect customs representative shall obtain the status of authorised CBAM declarant, irrespective of whether the importer is exempted from the obligations under this Regulation pursuant to Article 2a.» A declarant may hand the filing to another: «An authorised CBAM declarant may delegate the submission of CBAM declarations as referred to in Article 6 to a person acting on behalf and in the name of that authorised CBAM declarant. The authorised CBAM declarant shall remain responsible for compliance with the obligations applicable to it under this Regulation.» A law firm's summary adds: «Indirect customs representatives are liable for penalties when acting as authorised CBAM declarants, except where they act on behalf of an importer established in a Member State and have not agreed to act in that capacity.»

*Analytical inference:* the representative's position turns on two facts the text states, where the importer is established and whether the representative agreed to act as declarant; delegating the filing does not move responsibility. *Legal Confirmation Required:* which of these two facts holds for each client the business represents.

## 5. Authoritative Guidance Document Analysis

The Commission's tax and customs directorate reports on the start: «The Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) successfully entered into force on the  1 January 2026», in a news article with «Publication date 14 January 2026». It states how customs treats the new rules: «the validation of CBAM  authorisations for CBAM goods is enforced by Customs before Release for Free Circulation, including the monitoring of 50 tonnes threshold». And it gives counts: «More than 4100 CBAM economic operators successfully obtained CBAM authorized declarant status across EU prior to and immediately after 1 January 2026.» It ends with a call: «Economic operators who have not yet submitted their CBAM authorisation applications are strongly encouraged to do so as soon as possible via the CBAM Registry.»

*Analytical inference:* customs checks the authorisation before release for free circulation, so a consignment lodged by a representative or importer without declarant status is held at that step; the page gives no processing time. *Legal Confirmation Required:* what a representative must show customs at lodging for goods below the threshold.

## 6. Anticipated Authoritative Guidance and Pending Regulatory Events

The text sets recurring and dated steps. Each year the Commission tests the threshold: «By 30 April of each calendar year, the Commission shall assess, on the basis of the import data for the preceding 12 calendar months, whether the single mass-based threshold ensures that paragraph 1 of this Article applies to no more than 1 % of the emissions embedded in the imported goods and processed products.» Verifiers register late: «The verifier shall submit the request for registration within two months of the date on which the accreditation was granted, but not before 1 September 2026.» Old certificates are cancelled: «on 1 November 2027, the Commission shall cancel any CBAM certificates purchased in respect of the embedded emissions for the year 2026». The law firm's summary lists further work: «Finally, a full review of the CBAM is planned before the end of 2025, in accordance with Article 30 of the CBAM Regulation, which requires the European Commission to present a report assessing the potential extension of the CBAM scope to additional products (e.g., organic chemicals and polymers, other precursors) and services (e.g., transportation services).» That planned date has passed, and the pages read do not report the review or its outcome.

*Analytical inference:* an extension of the mechanism to transport services would reach freight directly, but the summary calls it a report to assess, not a rule, so no duty on freight follows from it today. *Legal Confirmation Required:* the outcome of that review, which the pages read do not report.

## 7. Threshold Questions

The question is whether an importer is below the small-importer line: «Where the net mass of all goods imported by an importer in a given calendar year does not cumulatively exceed the single mass-based threshold, such an importer, including any importer with the status of an authorised CBAM declarant, should be exempted in a given calendar year from the obligations under Regulation (EU) 2023/956». Crossing it reaches every import of the year: «Where, within the relevant calendar year, an importer, including any importer with the status of an authorised CBAM declarant, exceeds the single mass-based threshold, the importer or the authorised CBAM declarant shall be subject to all obligations under this Regulation in respect of all emissions embedded in all goods imported in that calendar year.» Electricity and hydrogen sit outside the test: «Imports of electricity or hydrogen should therefore not be included under the de minimis exemption.»

*Analytical inference:* a client that imports near the line can cross it during the year, and the business that lodges for it then carries obligations on the whole year's goods; a representative that acts for several importers does not add their masses together, because the text tests the net mass per importer. *Legal Confirmation Required:* how the mass of goods lodged by a representative for several importers is attributed.

## 8. Substantive Requirements

Small importers. «An importer, including any importer with the status of an authorised CBAM declarant, shall be exempted from the obligations under this Regulation, where the net mass of the imported goods in a given calendar year does not cumulatively exceed the single mass-based threshold». «The exception applies to all importers, including those with authorised CBAM declarant status.»

Authorisation. «Any importer established in a Member State shall, prior to importing goods into the customs territory of the Union, apply for the status of authorised CBAM declarant». «such an importer or indirect customs representative may provisionally continue to import goods until the competent authority takes a decision under this Article» for applications filed by «by 31 March 2026».

Declaration and certificates. «By 30 September of each year, and for the first time in 2027 for the year 2026, each authorised CBAM declarant shall use the CBAM registry referred to in Article 14 to submit a CBAM declaration for the preceding calendar year.» «From 1 February 2027, a Member State shall sell CBAM certificates on a common central platform to authorised CBAM declarants established in that Member State.» «the Commission shall calculate the price of CBAM certificates that corresponds to the embedded emissions declared in respect of the year 2026».

Penalties. «An authorised CBAM declarant who fails to surrender, by 30 September of each year, the number of CBAM certificates that corresponds to the emissions embedded in goods imported during the preceding calendar year shall be held liable for the payment of a penalty.» «Such a penalty shall be identical to the excess emissions penalty set out in Article 16(3) of Directive 2003/87/EC». A law firm's summary puts the amounts: «Penalties for non-compliance are harmonised with the EU ETS excess emissions penalty regime (EUR 100 for each tonne of embedded emissions), with reductions possible for minor or unintentional errors.»

*Analytical inference:* the penalty falls on the declarant per certificate not surrendered, so for a representative acting as declarant it is a cost of the representative's own account; the Regulation states no pass-through to the client. *Legal Confirmation Required:* whether a representative may charge a client the certificates or the penalty under the services contract.

## 10. Registration and Reporting Obligations

The registry is the channel: «By 30 September of each year, and for the first time in 2027 for the year 2026, each authorised CBAM declarant shall use the CBAM registry referred to in Article 14 to submit a CBAM declaration for the preceding calendar year.» The application carries data: «estimated quantity of imports of goods into the customs territory of the Union by type of goods and information on the Member States of import, for the calendar year during which the application is submitted, and for the following calendar year». Customs data feeds the registry: «The information on the sale and repurchase of CBAM certificates in the common central platform shall be transferred to the CBAM registry at the end of each working day.»

*Analytical inference:* the application asks for an estimate of imports by type and Member State, so a representative applying for status needs client import forecasts for two calendar years. *Legal Confirmation Required:* whether the business files the application itself or each client does.

## 11. Operational System Requirements

COST ALERT: the business needs a record of which client imports it lodges as representative and which certificates sit in each declarant account. The quarterly rule is «From 2027, the authorised CBAM declarant shall ensure that the number of CBAM certificates on its account in the CBAM registry at the end of each quarter corresponds to at least 50 % of the embedded emissions in all goods it has imported since the beginning of the calendar year». And the rule on the account at surrender: «The authorised CBAM declarant shall ensure that the required number of CBAM certificates is available on its account in the CBAM registry.» The Commission's page shows that customs is wired to the registry: «10483 Import Customs Declarations with CBAM goods» «were validated automatically and in real time via integrated customs systems».

*Analytical inference:* a business that acts as declarant needs, per client and per quarter, the imported mass, the country of origin and the CN code, because the holding rule refers to the goods imported since the start of the year. *Legal Confirmation Required:* whether default values or actual values apply to each client's goods.

## 12. Exemptions and Edge Cases

Beyond the small-importer exemption: «By way of derogation from paragraphs 1 and 2, this Regulation shall not apply to goods to be moved or used in the context of military activities pursuant to Article 1, point (49), of Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2015/2446». Offshore energy is excluded: «electricity generated on the continental shelf or in the exclusive economic zone of a Member State or of a country or territory listed in points 1 and 2 of Annex III». A penalty can be cut: «where an importer exceeded the single mass-based threshold by no more than 10 % of that threshold».

*Analytical inference:* each exclusion is tied to a stated condition and none covers freight in general. *Legal Confirmation Required:* whether a consignment moved for armed forces falls in the military exclusion.

## 13. Adjacent Industry Research and Alternatives

A briefing paper from a policy research institute, «Marta Kulesza June 2025», written before the amending Regulation, states: «This is a critical year as CBAM shifts from a transitional phase to full implementation» On trade effects it says: «CBAM’s direct trade impact has been limited so far, but long-term effects may include reduced EU imports»

*Analytical inference:* the stated direct trade impact and long-term effects of the paper concern trade between the EU and third countries, not the duties of a customs representative; it gives no freight rate effect. *Legal Confirmation Required:* whether any of its stated long-term effects bears on the goods a client imports.

   "body": "## 1. Purpose and Scope of This Document

This document covers «DIRECTIVE (EU) 2023/1791 OF THE EUROPEAN PARLIAMENT AND OF THE COUNCIL of 13 September 2023 on energy efficiency and amending Regulation (EU) 2023/955 (recast)», the recast of the Energy Efficiency Directive. Where this directive applies: the Member States of the Union, because «This Directive is addressed to the Member States.» Its scope is set out as: «Article 1 Subject matter and scope 1. This Directive establishes a common framework of measures to promote energy efficiency within the Union». What the Directive says is stated from its own text; what it means for a freight business is marked *Analytical inference:* and each point for counsel is marked *Legal Confirmation Required:*.

## 2. What This Regulation Is and Why It Applies to the Workspace

The Directive is the Union's framework for using less energy: «This Directive establishes a common framework of measures to promote energy efficiency within the Union in order to ensure that the Union’s targets on energy efficiency are met and enables further energy efficiency improvements.» It sets a floor, not a ceiling: «The requirements laid down in this Directive are minimum requirements and shall not prevent any Member State from maintaining or introducing more stringent measures.» The headline target: «Member States shall collectively ensure a reduction of energy consumption of at least 11,7 % in 2030 compared to the projections of the 2020 EU Reference Scenario so that the Union’s final energy consumption amounts to no more than 763 Mtoe.» It replaces the earlier energy efficiency directive: «Directive 2012/27/EU, as amended by the acts listed in Part A of Annex XVI is repealed with effect from 12 October 2025»

The directive enters into force as Article 39 says: «This Directive shall enter into force on the twentieth day following that of its publication in the Official Journal of the European Union .» The text counts its delegation period from 10 October 2023, and the main national measures are due earlier than most dates below: «Member States shall bring into force the laws, regulations and administrative provisions necessary to comply with Articles 1, 2 and 3, Article 4(1) to (4), Article 4(5), first, second, fourth, fifth and sixth subparagraphs, Article 4(6) and (7), Articles 5 to 11, Article 12(2) to (5), Articles 21 to 25, Article 26(1), (2) and (4) to (14), Article 27, Article 28(1) to (5), Articles 29 to 32 and Annexes I, III to VII, X, XI and XV by 11 October 2025.»

*Analytical inference:* the Directive reaches a freight business in two ways the text shows: as an enterprise whose energy use passes the thresholds of Article 11, and as a supplier of services to public bodies under Article 7. The Directive places each duty on Member States, which pass national law.

## 3. Issues Requiring Immediate Action

MONITORING: the only audit date in the text, the first energy audit date for enterprises above 10 TJ, is past; the next fixed date is in 2027 and the duties sit on Member States. «Member States shall ensure that the enterprises referred to in the first subparagraph carry out a first energy audit by 11 October 2026 and that subsequent energy audits are carried out at least every four years.» The next fixed date is the management system: «Member States shall ensure that the enterprises referred to in the first subparagraph have an energy management system in place at the latest by 11 October 2027.»

- A compliance lead, this month, totals the business's energy use for the last three years across every energy carrier it uses (the fuel and electricity of its sites and vehicles) in each Member State where it operates, converts it to terajoules and compares it with the two thresholds in the text: 10 TJ for an energy audit and 85 TJ for an energy management system.
- A compliance lead asks, for each Member State above the 10 TJ line, whether national law implementing Article 11 is in force and which authority is responsible, and books an energy audit by a qualified or accredited expert where the business is above 10 TJ and has no certified management system.

*Analytical inference:* both steps rest on Article 11, which tells Member States to ensure these duties on enterprises; the Directive does not say whether a forwarder is above either threshold. *Legal Confirmation Required:* whether the business counts as an enterprise above 10 TJ or 85 TJ in each Member State, which national measure applies, and whether the first audit date of 11 October 2026 is already missed there.

## 4. How the Workspace Sits in the Compliance Chain

The Directive is addressed to Member States and names several parties: enterprises, contracting authorities and contracting entities, owners and operators of data centres, and the competent authority. Member States ensure the enterprise duties: «Member States shall ensure that enterprises with an average annual consumption higher than 85 TJ of energy over the previous three years, taking all energy carriers together, implement an energy management system.» Public buyers are bound by Article 7: «Member States shall ensure that contracting authorities and contracting entities, when concluding public contracts and concessions with a value equal to or greater than the thresholds laid down in Article 8 of Directive 2014/23/EU, Article 4 of Directive 2014/24/EU and Article 15 of Directive 2014/25/EU, purchase only products, services buildings and works with high energy-efficiency performance in accordance with the requirements referred to in Annex IV to this Directive, unless it is not technically feasible.» A forwarder is not named.

*Analytical inference:* a forwarder falls under Article 11 as an enterprise when its own energy use passes the thresholds, and meets Article 7 as a seller of services to a public buyer. *Legal Confirmation Required:* which entity in a corporate group is the enterprise whose consumption is counted, and whether a transport service sold to a public body is a service with a high energy-efficiency performance requirement under Annex IV.

## 5. Authoritative Guidance Document Analysis

*No content for this section as of November 2026: no authoritative guidance document is held for this Directive.*

## 6. Anticipated Authoritative Guidance and Pending Regulatory Events

The text sets Commission steps that can change the rules. Thresholds for the energy efficiency first test: «By 11 October 2027, the Commission shall carry out an assessment of the thresholds set out in paragraph 1, with the aim of downward revision» followed by «The Commission shall, by 11 October 2028, submit a report to the European Parliament and to the Council» A review of the whole Directive: «By 28 February 2027 and every five years thereafter, the Commission shall evaluate the implementation of this Directive and submit a report to the European Parliament and to the Council.» A check against the 2030 targets: «By 31 October 2032, the Commission shall assess whether the Union has achieved its 2030 headline targets on energy efficiency.» Data centres, a date that has passed: «By 15 May 2025, the Commission shall assess the available data on the energy efficiency of data centres» Default coefficients: «By 25 December 2026 and every four years thereafter, the Commission shall revise the default coefficients on the basis of observed data.» «Those revisions shall be carried out taking into account its effects on Union law such as Directive 2009/125/EC and Regulation (EU) 2017/1369.» The power for delegated acts runs «The power to adopt delegated acts referred to in Article 33 shall be conferred on the Commission for a period of five years from 10 October 2023.»

*Analytical inference:* the 11 October 2027 assessment of the Article 3 thresholds points to lower thresholds, which would bring more Member State planning decisions under the energy efficiency test; the text states no result. The 28 February 2027 review is the next general point at which the Directive can change. After the 25 December 2026 revision of the default coefficients, a Member State that uses the default value will use the revised one, while one that notifies its own coefficient keeps doing so; the text states no new values, so the effect on any reported figure is not stated.

## 7. Threshold Questions

Whether Article 11 reaches a business is decided by its own energy use: «Member States shall ensure that enterprises with an average annual consumption higher than 85 TJ of energy over the previous three years, taking all energy carriers together, implement an energy management system.» and «Member States shall ensure that enterprises with an average annual consumption higher than 10 TJ of energy over the previous three years, taking all energy carriers together, which do not implement an energy management system are subject to an energy audit.» Whether Article 3 reaches a project is decided by its value: «Member States shall ensure that energy efficiency solutions, including demand-side resources and system flexibilities, are assessed in planning, policy and major investment decisions of a value of more than EUR 100 000 000 each or EUR 175 000 000 for transport infrastructure projects» Whether a data centre report is due is decided by its size: «By 15 May 2024 and every year thereafter, Member States shall require owners and operators of data centres in their territory with a power demand of the installed information technology (IT) of at least 500kW, to make the information set out in Annex VII publicly available, except for information subject to Union and national law protecting trade and business secrets and confidentiality.»

*Analytical inference:* the energy use is counted over the previous three years and across all energy carriers together, so fuel for vehicles counts alongside electricity. *Legal Confirmation Required:* whether the measure for a given enterprise uses the group or the individual company, and the year from which the three-year period is counted.

## 8. Substantive Requirements

Scope. «Article 1 Subject matter and scope 1. This Directive establishes a common framework of measures to promote energy efficiency within the Union»

Target. «Member States shall collectively ensure a reduction of energy consumption of at least 11,7 % in 2030 compared to the projections of the 2020 EU Reference Scenario so that the Union’s final energy consumption amounts to no more than 763 Mtoe.»

Savings each year. «new savings each year from 1 January 2021 to 31 December 2030 of:» The rates for the periods run: «0,8 % of annual final energy consumption from 1 January 2021 to 31 December 2023»; «1,3 % of annual final energy consumption from 1 January 2024 to 31 December 2025»; «1,5 % of annual final energy consumption from 1 January 2026 to 31 December 2027»; and «1,9 % of annual final energy consumption from 1 January 2028 to 31 December 2030» «Member States shall continue to achieve new annual savings in accordance with the savings rate provided for in point (b)(iv) of the first subparagraph for ten-year periods after 2030.» The way Member States reach them: «Member States shall achieve the amount of energy savings required under paragraph 1 of this Article either by establishing an energy efficiency obligation scheme as referred to in Article 9 or by adopting alternative policy measures as referred to in Article 10.»

Management systems and audits. «Member States shall ensure that enterprises with an average annual consumption higher than 85 TJ of energy over the previous three years, taking all energy carriers together, implement an energy management system.» «The energy management system shall be certified by an independent body, in accordance with the relevant European or international standards.» «Member States shall ensure that the enterprises referred to in the first subparagraph have an energy management system in place at the latest by 11 October 2027.» «Member States shall ensure that enterprises with an average annual consumption higher than 10 TJ of energy over the previous three years, taking all energy carriers together, which do not implement an energy management system are subject to an energy audit.» «Member States shall ensure that the enterprises referred to in the first subparagraph carry out a first energy audit by 11 October 2026 and that subsequent energy audits are carried out at least every four years.» «The enterprises concerned shall draw up a concrete and feasible Action Plan on the basis of the recommendations arising from those energy audits.» «Member States shall ensure that the Action Plans and the recommendation implementation rate are published in the enterprise’s annual report, and that they are made publicly available, subject to Union and national law protecting trade and business secrets and confidentiality.»

Audit content. «be based on up-to-date, measured, traceable operational data on energy consumption and (for electricity) load profiles;» «comprise a detailed review of the energy consumption profile of buildings or groups of buildings, industrial operations or installations, including transportation;»

Public procurement. «Member States shall ensure that contracting authorities and contracting entities, when concluding public contracts and concessions with a value equal to or greater than the thresholds laid down in Article 8 of Directive 2014/23/EU, Article 4 of Directive 2014/24/EU and Article 15 of Directive 2014/25/EU, purchase only products, services buildings and works with high energy-efficiency performance in accordance with the requirements referred to in Annex IV to this Directive, unless it is not technically feasible.» «The obligations referred to in paragraph 1 of this Article shall not apply if they undermine public security or impede the response to public health emergencies.»

Data centres. «By 15 May 2024 and every year thereafter, Member States shall require owners and operators of data centres in their territory with a power demand of the installed information technology (IT) of at least 500kW, to make the information set out in Annex VII publicly available, except for information subject to Union and national law protecting trade and business secrets and confidentiality.» «Paragraph 1 shall not apply to data centres used for, or providing their services exclusively with the final aim of, defence and civil protection.»

Penalties. «Member States shall lay down the rules on penalties applicable to infringements of national provisions adopted pursuant to this Directive and shall take all measures necessary to ensure that they are implemented. The penalties provided for shall be effective, proportionate and dissuasive.»

*Analytical inference:* each duty falls on a Member State, which passes it to enterprises, public buyers and data centre operators through national law; the Directive states no pass-through of energy savings cost to a customer or forwarder. The savings rates rise from 0,8 % to 1,9 % of annual final energy consumption, so the national measures tighten over the periods.

*Legal Confirmation Required:* which national measure puts Article 11 on the business, and whether any penalty set under Article 32 applies to a forwarder or its client.

*No content for this section as of November 2026: the Directive sets energy efficiency rules for Member States and enterprises, not rules for products a freight business sells.*

## 10. Registration and Reporting Obligations

Enterprises above the threshold are known to the authorities: «Member States shall ensure that that information is made available to the national authorities responsible for implementation of this Article.» The plan and its progress are public: «Member States shall ensure that the Action Plans and the recommendation implementation rate are published in the enterprise’s annual report, and that they are made publicly available, subject to Union and national law protecting trade and business secrets and confidentiality.» The competent authority: «Member States shall designate a competent authority or body to ensure that the timelines for conducting energy audits set out in paragraph 2 of this Article are complied with and the minimum criteria set out in Annex VI are correctly applied.» Data centre operators report in public: «By 15 May 2024 and every year thereafter, Member States shall require owners and operators of data centres in their territory with a power demand of the installed information technology (IT) of at least 500kW, to make the information set out in Annex VII publicly available, except for information subject to Union and national law protecting trade and business secrets and confidentiality.» Member States report to the Commission on penalties, a date that has passed: «Member States shall by 11 October 2025 notify the Commission of those rules and of those measures»

*Analytical inference:* an enterprise above 10 TJ has a reporting trail: consumption information to the national authority, an Action Plan and its implementation rate in the annual report. *Legal Confirmation Required:* the national platform, if any, to which consumption above the thresholds is reported.

## 11. Operational System Requirements

MONITORING: the audit rests on measured data, so the data has to exist before the audit. The audit minimum criteria: «be based on up-to-date, measured, traceable operational data on energy consumption and (for electricity) load profiles;» and it reviews «comprise a detailed review of the energy consumption profile of buildings or groups of buildings, industrial operations or installations, including transportation;»

- An energy data owner sets up a measured, traceable record of fuel and electricity use per site and per vehicle group, kept for several years, so that a first audit or a management system can start from it.
- A finance or reporting lead adds the Action Plan and the recommendation implementation rate to the annual report process, since the text has both published in the annual report subject to confidentiality law.

*Analytical inference:* because the audit review names transportation, the energy of transportation sits inside the audit, not only buildings. *Legal Confirmation Required:* whether a third-party carrier's fuel counts towards the business's own consumption.

## 12. Exemptions and Edge Cases

Some cases are outside. Public buyers: «The obligations referred to in paragraph 1 of this Article shall not apply if they undermine public security or impede the response to public health emergencies.» Data centres: «Paragraph 1 shall not apply to data centres used for, or providing their services exclusively with the final aim of, defence and civil protection.» Smaller businesses: «Member States shall develop programmes with the aim of encouraging and providing technical support to SMEs that are not subject to paragraph 1 or 2 to undergo energy audits»

*Analytical inference:* a business below 10 TJ is not required by Article 11 to have an audit, but Member States run programmes for smaller businesses. *Legal Confirmation Required:* whether the business qualifies as a small or medium-sized enterprise in each Member State.
